summary:
Gyeonggi Province stands under the national framework of South Korea, and the national assessment applies alongside the province-specific findings below. The sources yield no Gyeonggi-specific rule on criminal exposure, entry, identity documents, screening, facilities or healthcare access; what they document is a provincial protection instrument covering students.

Gyeonggi-do enacted South Korea's first student human rights ordinance in 2010. The ordinance provides non-discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, which are the provisions most contested in the 2024-26 repeal wave against student-rights ordinances elsewhere in the country. Gyeonggi-do and Seoul are the only two jurisdictions whose ordinances also include a right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy.

The ordinance is administered rather than dormant. The Superintendent of Public Instruction conducts an annual survey on student human rights, and the province marks a Student Human Rights Day.

Its durability is the live question. On 28 April 2024 the Seoul Metropolitan Council abolished the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after the Seoul office adopted it, following an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to the ordinance's sexual-orientation clause and pushed through by the ruling People Power Party council. At that date six regional education offices, Gyeonggi among them, still enforced comparable ordinances, and a Gyeonggi-based teacher quoted in the reporting defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition. The Seoul model was itself first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province, so the repeal movement has targeted the province's own template.
tangentialFactors:
The repeal pressure documented in Seoul is directed at the clause structure Gyeonggi's ordinance pioneered. The August 2022 campaign that preceded abolition in Seoul was organised by religious groups and parents specifically against the sexual-orientation provision, and the same clause set is described as the most disputed element of student-rights ordinances across the 2024-26 repeal wave. Gyeonggi's ordinance carries that clause as the originating model.

Set against that, Gyeonggi's education office was one of six regional bodies still enforcing a comparable ordinance as of 28 April 2024, and the province's ordinance is one of only two in the country to add pregnancy to its non-discrimination grounds. The reported defence of the ordinance came from a teacher working in Gyeonggi, indicating organised local support as well as organised opposition elsewhere.
localsOnly:
Students within Gyeonggi Province are covered by an ordinance that bars discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and the province is one of only two jurisdictions extending that protection to pregnancy.

The provincial education authority operationalises the ordinance through an annual survey on student human rights conducted by the Superintendent of Public Instruction, and the province observes a Student Human Rights Day.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the opposition-led National Assembly followed through on its stated intention to legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions is unresolved in the sources; the commitment is recorded, the outcome is not.

Whether Gyeonggi Province itself faces a repeal campaign of the kind mounted in Seoul from August 2022 onward is not sourced. The inventory records only that the province still enforced its ordinance at April 2024 and that a local teacher defended it.

No region-specific signal on criminalisation, legal gender recognition, identity documents, border screening, restroom or facility access, healthcare provision, or partner recognition was identified for Gyeonggi in this inventory. Those layers sit with the national record.
